I wish the author had dug more into nutritional requirements, scientific studies, food trials and nutrient guides related to pet food and spoken to vets specializing in pet nutrition. It feels like there is so much marketing noise to cut through.

This site has information about boutique diets and heart disease - which has been increasing with the rise of boutique diets:
https://hospital.vetmed.wsu.edu/2026/01/14/boutique-diets-and-heart-disease/

Food that has been AAFCO food trialled long term has had direct study of its long term effects. This standard is not the same as food made according to AAFCO standard but not trialled, which is the majority of food sold. Home cooking is a wildcard. 

Having had older rescue dogs with various gastro and heart issues, and trying a wide variety of commercial and home cooked options, a note to folks about home cooking - depending on the food and ratio it is easy to make tasty food that is accidentally nutritionally incomplete. Depending on the ingredients and ratios you will likely need to add a dog specific nutritional supplement to ensure the food is nutritionally complete - getting it right can be more complex/nuanced than expected.

comments.name: Kim Aubry
comments.body:
I have two very specific memories of ZABARs (yes we went there a lot growing up on 100th Street).
First is, every spring our dad would stop there on his way home the day he heard through the grapevine that “Les fraises des boit “ had arrived. On just one date in early June a jet plane from France would bring in just picked alpine strawberries from France and we had a go, with whipped cream. Imagine! The ZABAR family knew there were Frenchie immigrants who missed this treat from home. Fabulous. Turns out years later I learned they aren’t even in the same genus as domestic strawberries they are their own thing. Tiny. Like eating perfume!
My other memory much more nerdy. The bakery and deli were across the store from the checkout. When you ordered your bread and cheese and lox and herring they would put them in a bag with a hook and then put the hook on this rotating spiral rod on the ceiling. It would convey your bag of stuff across the store to the cash register SLOWLY. But by the time you walked across the store to the checkout your order would arrive JUST IN TIME for you to pay. I thought it was magic.

comments.body: After growing up in NYC, I moved to SF. After a visit back home, my father (may he rest in peace) drove me to JFK and, as we said goodbye, handed me a bag with a dozen bagels, lox, whitefish, sable and two kinds of cream cheese. He said, "I stopped by Zabars before we left and thought you might like to have this when you get back to Calif". I said thank you, gave him a kiss, headed to my flight. Boarding I put the Zabar's bag in the overhead bin. Mid way through the flight someone opened the overhead to retreive something and (I guess) the cabin pressurization turned that overhead bin and my Zabars bag of goodies into a bagel and smoked fish aroma, scent, ambrosia that wafted thoughtout the entire plane. I popped up, embarassed, and grabbed the bag to see if there was anything I could do to stem the bagel bouquet from doing any more olfactory damage. Pulling the Zabars bag from the overhead bin, I turned to the packed plane and whispered "sorry" while at least ten people smiled and whispered back "Zabars" with looks that cried out understanding, envy. For a second I thought about opening the bag and sharing everything Dad bought as atonement, but thought better of that idea and I sheepishly repacked the bin and quickly sat down again.

I've also had the pleasure of helping rescue some of these birds by either calling or bringing them in to the team at Pacific Wildlife Care (referenced in the article) in Morro Bay who are working overtime to help save as many birds as they can. If you find a weak bird on the beach in Morro Bay, Los Osos, or Cayucos call PWC's hotline at (805)-543-9453. If they can't send any volunteers to come help, they also encourage you to bring the bird in yourself using towels or a bird carrying box (be careful to wear protective gear though since their beaks can be sharp when pecking!). This article brings back memories of my father. I grew up in the UK and we often spent our annual holiday on the Isle of Wight. One morning my dad woke me very early to watch the SS United States sail up the Solent on the way to Southampton. He told me how she was the fastest ship in the world and everything else he had read about her. What I remember to this day is how she sparkled in the morning sun. comments.name: meirman
comments.body: I think Monty Halls answer was correct and the mathematicians is incorrect. if you open one door and it's empty that raises the odds that the first store he he chose is correct to 50% and if he switches it will also be 50%. The table at the end is misleading because it combines the two error situations into one line. If they were separate lines, you would have six errors and six successes, 50%. Or you could combine two of the error lines for each of the three original choices, and then there would be four error lines and four success lines, again 50%. I'd say that the statistician was wrong.

comments.body: Finally I get it. comments.name: Russell
comments.body: When I was an Assistant Professor of Molecular and Cell Biology at Berkeley in the late 2000s, I sought out Steve Selvin to give my lab some statistical advice. I had no idea he was the originator of the Monty Hall problem! But quite coincidentally I happened to mention to him my love of the Monty Hall problem. Imagine my surprise when he told me that he was, in fact, the originator of that problem! I was so enthused, he actually opened up his file cabinet and retrieved a letter that he had received from Monty Hall himself dated May 12, 1975. He made me a copy of the letter that I still have. The letter said: "Although I am not a student of statistics, I do know that these figures can always be used to one's advantage...And if you ever get on my show, the rules hold fast for you -- no trading boxes after the selection. Next time let's play on my home grounds. I graduated in chemistry and zoology. You want to know your chances of surviving with our polluted air and water?". Anyway, Steve not only gave me a great story, but also some great statistical advice. I treasure that brief interaction as a great example of the amazing cast of characters one can run into at Berkeley. RIP Steve.

comments.name: Cory
comments.body: I have written extensively on the Monty Hall problem. the solution of course is to change doors. But virtually no one, other than Monty realized the central concept of the problem, which is prior knowledge. It's because Monty knows which door the prize is under and he can always show you the losing door. If Monty did not have prior knowledge your chances would be even and it would not pay to switch - but in that case Monty would show you the door with the prize one-third of the time and the game would be ruined. All the analysis and statistics, which are valid, do not mention this is the crux of the dilemma: Monty's prior knowledge of the right door. It is not a game of chance, rather perception

Speaking from the vantage point of a young-ish millennial, I find this trend both heartening and not at all surprising. Seeing a film in cinemas is a grounding, communal experience that comes with prosocial expectations: put your phone away, disengage from the online world, be mindful of your neighbors, and participate in a human experience with the people around you through the artistic medium of film; basic social and mental health hygiene of which we find ourselves routinely lacking in our age of meaningless distractions. At the same time, the barriers to participation are remarkably low, requiring little in the way of training or even social skill to engage. Film remains the first and undisputed champion of popular artforms.

Personally, I've seen 31 films this year thus far and find myself self-conscious of the fact that I'm regularly one of the oldest audience members, at the same time that I am relieved to see the future of cinema alive in the presence of my younger peers.

Nehru’s handling of the 1962 Sino-Indian border crisis remains one of the clearest examples of what happens when political idealism overrides cold military realism. By relying heavily on Gen. B.M. Kaul—a favorite whose personal proximity to the Prime Minister bypassed professional channels—the defense establishment fell into confirmation bias. Sidelining generals who warned of poor supply lines, artillery deficits, and terrain realities to push the 'Forward Policy' under Kaul's command led directly to the tragedy at Namka Chu. The tragic hubris of the Nehru-Gandhi line lies in confusing dynastic entitlement with political wisdom. 

While Jawaharlal Nehru earned his mantle through decades of struggle, sacrifice, and intellectual rigor during the independence movement, his successors inherited power as a birthright rather than winning it through grassroots political maturity.

This fundamental disconnect manifested in catastrophic misreadings of history and deep-seated emotional realities. 

Indira Gandhi treated Punjab not as a sacred socio-religious powder keg with a distinct ethos, but as a chessboard for political maneuvering—culminating in the tragic desecration of Operation Blue Star and the violent spiral that followed. 

Years later, Rajiv Gandhi repeated this fatal error in Sri Lanka, mistaking a deeply emotional Tamil ethnic movement for a routine law-and-order problem. By deploying the IPKF without understanding the ground realities, New Delhi alienated both sides of the conflict and sent over a thousand Indian soldiers to their deaths in a war that wasn't theirs.

When leaders substitute sane counsel and historical literacy with dynastic arrogance, the outcome is inevitably disastrous. Folly rushed in where wisdom dreaded to tread—and ultimately, the tragic assassinations of both Prime Ministers were the bitter harvest of failing to comprehend the very people and conflicts they sought to command.

Surprises in Nature abound. Bumblebees shouldn't be able to fly, but they do. Microbes shouldn't be able to survive in such extreme environments as hot springs, hydrothermal vents, salt flats or deep sea trenches--but they do. There are lizards that walk on water, mushrooms in Chernobyl that "eat" radiation, and jellyfish that can live forever. 

As we search for signs of biology on other worlds we should remain mindful of the limits of our knowledge. The most important discoveries that await us may remain stubbornly hidden if we lack the imagination to see them.

I suspect the government is happy to let the monarch take the heat.

By complete chance, I met the man once, while in college in about 1977.  My dorm had an international focus and we were on a prominent Ag campus.  Charles, pre-Diana, was coming to visit, and my dorm, which had a regular speaker program, was selected to send a small delegation to meet him at the Food Sciences Building, apparently counting on us not to cause an an international incident.

The choice was apparently not an accident.  The prince was allowed some latitude his interests, and Charles had lifelong interests in advancing British agriculture and food sufficiency, and promoting classic architectural and construction with an eye towards long life, environmental impact and energy efficiency.

In our few minutes with him I got some definite impressions.  He seemed an introvert forced by duty into an extremely public job, and doing an honest job of it, being attentive and focused on half a dozen US undergrads.  But it must have seemed a slog through a life he didn’t choose.  At least he finally got the girl.

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
Reading your piece, Mr. Risen--

--I was reminded of my daughter. 

She had written a paper and asked me to look it over.  

So I did.  And suggested she change this.  And that.  And something over here.  And over there.  Until--

--she pulled it out of my hands.  

"Dad," she remonstrated.  "It's my paper."  

"It's your name," said the late Mr. Fisketjon, "that appears on the title page."  

Precisely!  And there's the mark of a conscientious editor. To clear away the clutter, correct the blunders, add that last little bit of clarity--

--that'll make a book what it wants to be.  The book it was meant to be---

--without shaping it into the book YOU would write.  If you were writing a book--

--but you're not.  The author is.  It's his book.  

And Mr. Fisketjon seems to have learned this lesson to perfection.  Devoted as he was to improving, sharpening, clarifying.  And then at the last possible moment--

--stepping out of the way.  Letting the author speak in his own voice.  Letting the author bring out his own book.  

And so many of these books, I gather--

--were extraordinarily fine.  

What a man! 

Thanks, Mr. Risen.

You start to build a small library of matching spines filled with titles by authors who come to shape your taste for literature, give contour to your ambition and define your worldview. A decade later you find yourself in caverns on Avenue C telling yourself you are not the kind of guy who would be in a place like this at this time of the morning. comments.name: Jeanine

This story brought to mind a story reported in 1993 by Susan Stamberg on NPR's Weekend Edition. I consider that one of the finest - and most moving - pieces of journalism ever. 

Ms. Stambeg accompanied the National Symphony Orchestra when it traveled to Moscow and performed before a crowd on 100,000 in Red Square... Mstislav Rostropovich, age 90, returning to Russia following years in exile. Logistics and travel challenges. Bitter cold that required the NSO's extraordinary musicians to play in fingerless gloves. And all this with the backdrop - just across town - of the Russian White House under siege following Boris Yeltsin's dissolution of the Parliament just days earlier. 

In a time of tumult and global unpredictability, Sergey Kislyak, then the Russian ambassador to the United States, described the NSO tour as, “one of the brightest elements in our current relations.” 

Bravo! to the power of music to unite a world in conflict. Thank you to all whose dedication makes this happen. And eternal thanks to Ms. Stamberg who never let us forget our common humanity.

comments.body: Collecting “art” isn’t hard, if you open up the definition, and look outside the boundaries.  Any image that attracts you can be framed, and that frame can be from a second hand store, or inexpensive ready made off the rack at a framing shop.  I’ve re- framed postcards, old prints removed from dated/ugly past lives, and my favorite, an old guest list from the cruise ship carrying my father’s  family to China in 1922. Mix in any objects  of interest, and have fun.  Keep a tube of spackle and a can of your wall paint handy to easily repaired old hanger holes when moving different pieces in and out over time. Check out the PublicDomain.org website for their fantastic and reasonably priced selection of quality prints of every subject imaginable.

They don’t have to be expensive. I don’t think you can make your space look you’ve been collecting over time by throwing a bunch of stuff up on a wall. I have some family portraits, things I inherited from my parents, pieces friends made, photos I had enlarged & framed, items from museum shops or even brochures from exhibitions.  Every piece moves me in some way & I can change them or take something down if I want to. It’s ok to have blank space while you find the right item.

comments.name: Laura Grand

When I wanted to create a gallery wall, I went around my house and took things off the walls from every room, saw what I had available, laid it out on the floor to see what looked good together and in what arrangement, filled in some gaps with plates and a barometer, then hung them on the wall. I was able to make a convincing gallery wall just "shopping" from my own house. The pieces I didn't use for my gallery wall I redistributed in other rooms.

Sure, I have some empty spots throughout the rest of the house, but that's okay, and now if I find something I really like I have somewhere to put it.

comments.body: I have been to Vietnam three times since 1998. Once to bring my son home from his orphanage in DaNang, again in 2000 to bring his sister home from her orphanage in Hoa Binh a province a few hours outside of Hanoi and again in 2011 to see their homeland and be introduced to their birth mothers and families each time. It was a fascinating experience the beaches we ended up seeing were China Beach outside of Da Nang and in Nha Trang. It was so hard to believe how much change had occurred in this beautiful country over those years. The golf courses set into the mountains in the north were stunning. We saw so much development going on. It made me sad. I guess that’s progress. We did stay in a waterfront resort in Nha Trang our last time there. The water was quite laden with trash, Dumped from cruise ships I imagine. Vietnam will always hold a special place in my heart since my two beautiful children now adults were born there.

comments.name: The Alamo Kid
comments.body:
In 1969 I was working as a civilian with a nonprofit medical group treating war-injured Vietnamese women and children in the Saigon area (locals today still call the city 'Saigon' not the official 'Ho Chi Minh City').

The war was raging and times were hectic.  When we needed a break, if work permitted, a group of us (Vietnamese, Australian, American) would head for a couple of days at the beach 60 miles to the east.

Vung Tau was the nearest established beachside R&R (Rest and Relaxation) city -- and guarded by a heavy presence of South Vietnamese troops.  But the hotels were expensive even then for our meager budget.  And the beaches crowded.

So instead we headed 15 miles up the coast to Long Hai -- with two almost deserted hotels and miles of beautiful unpopulated beaches. 

The hitch?  Long Hai was unguarded and at night the area was controlled by the Viet Cong.  We were told the hotel owners had paid off the V.C. to leave guests alone and at peace.

But the room prices were still steep for us.  So we decided to chance it and sleep on the sand dunes away from the hotels.

We were antsy and a little afraid.  We plotted how if the V.C. came we'd sprint into the waves and hope to disappear in the darkness.  It was a beautiful, moonlit night and I'm sure the V.C. must have known we were there -- but left us alone as we were civilians.  When the sun rose gloriously over the sea the next morning -- we were relieved.

No such concerns today.  Peace is so much better than war.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body:
I'm not a seafood lover (having been terrified and hospitalised twice in childhood with fish bones painfully stuck in my throat)

but a favourite memory in Vietnam was riding a rented scooter to a beach resort, just north of Nha Trang, which I found deserted in winter, so I just sat on the beach, alone

and was almost immediately approached by a local woman wearing the pointed hat, carrying a small wok, and offering prawns/shrimp

Her quoted price was not high, so I accepted more for the experience, and perhaps because she was so persuasive

And within a few minutes she had fired up some flames and cooked some prawns to a smoky flavour in the wok, which I then enjoyed eating before she walked away.

I don't like wet, slippery seafood - but this was dry and smoky - and delicious - as well as a lifetime memory - sitting in the sand on an empty beach, and having some seafood cooked to order, beside me on the sand.  Bliss.

Pollution seems to thin these birds out. Once on the way back home we witnessed about 20 eagles waiting for the tide to go out enough to catch their food. They were sitting on sagging communications lines stretched over a bay. You don’t see that too often anymore. The nest in Big Bear is a great tool to show kids how to respect Nature. We have been watching since 2024, my grandkids have been watching much longer. It’s a close up look at the hard work and other skills eagles use to communicate. This year when Jackie died I wasn’t sure the kids should get too involved. In the final autopsy Jackie’s system was full of toxins. Sadly you can complain but the pollution continues. Big Bear has a large firework show that is a major pollution event. The lake is small with a large amount of housing more pollution potential and habitat degradation. They may bring back an endangered species but how can it be sustained? I am hoping this next eagle couple will be successful, at least one more time.

comments.name: Tim Barrus
comments.body: I care about the writing. Why do you put so much cultural energy into the writer. Human beings do not interest me. I care about the work. The writing is the work. Most people in marketing will care about the writer. They do not know how to care about a book. They do not know how to care about writing. Making people care about the writer -- versus what the writer does -- is the epitome of sheer laziness. You just focus on a life and the inevitable failures of that life. It cannot be a literary life without hatreds and failure. There are a million ways to tell the story of a writer. But it takes a lot more work and a lot more creativity to find the soul of a book and run with it. The disingenuousness gets played out when you discover that the writer is a human being, too, and his work is his work. Writing is work. Janet Malcolm was one of the hardest working journalists in history. Biography itself is mainly garbage. Biographers walk around inside heads fully self-empowered to get everything right. Wrong. I had to stop reading biography. How many agendas can one reader absorb. "Janet Malcolm was mainly known for her work." Why even bother writing that when you have no intention of focusing on the work because you are more interested in the writer than what the writer wrote. "And she remarked..." I do not care what she remarked. Writer's lives are messy and we get to cluck and dish and gossip. Biography is all cluck, all dish, and all stupid gossip. Writers are not their work.

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
Fascinating!  The more so because--

--knowing how readily we let fall an unguarded comment--

--Ms. Malcolm was careful to write out her answers.  

And the novelist Vladimir Nabokov?  He did exactly the same thing. 

He was interviewed once.  And did it on the fly.  Without duly weighing what came out of his mouth.  

And, of course--

--he was horrified to read what he'd said. 

But I cannot agree with Ms. Malcolm when she spoke so slightingly of people who interview people.  

What would be the alternative?  That we all sit there, huddled up in an uncommunicative silence?  Never answering questions.  Never called to account.  Never taking the trouble to explain who we are.  What we did.  Why we did it.

And yes!  A man or woman (on some level) is in the hands of the interviewer.  Who can shape the encounter as she likes.  And I guess Janet Malcolm did just that.  

But a verse from the New Testament comes to mind.  

"Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh."  

Which is to say:  on another level, the stuff I blurt out might well BE the person I am.  And I might not enjoy so bald, so uncompromising a revelation of myself.  

But a revelation it would be.  This, ladies and gentlemen--this is what I am.  And the totality of my life, everything I said or did or hoped to do--

--flows from that underlying reality.  

And this I guess Janet Malcolm realized to perfection. 

And arranged her life accordingly.  

Thanks, Ms. Szalai.

comments.name: David Robertson
comments.body:
"Let us consider the waiter in the café. His movement is quick and forward, a little too precise, a little too rapid... he is playing at being a waiter in a café" -- Jean-Paul Sartre, on denying reality, or "bad faith." In a sense, both Janet Malcolm and Eve Sneider are bad waiters. 

Malcolm wrote a biography about Sylvia Plath, The Silent Woman, which is actually about Malcolm's thoughts on writing a biography. Sneider writes a biography about Janet Malcolm, The Absent Woman, which she describes as  actually being a biography only "in theory."  I suggest we tip a decent fifteen percent, and we never come back to this place again.

I'm a cultural writer, luxury editor and novelist who also writes a blog about the power dynamic in culture. Power in itself, like everything else, is neither good nor bad. How we perceive it depends on the context.

There are those who use it to help others and those who exploit it only to enrich themselves.

But sooner or later, everyone comes to realize that the reason power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely is because you have to maintain power and to do that you have to acquire more. It's like an addict who needs a greater fix for the same effect — a case of the law of diminishing returns and a no-win situation.

Power is the opposite of freedom. That may seem counterintuitive,  but those who have the least are the most free, because they have little or nothing to lose.  Also, when you are busy acquiring power, you're not busy being creative and making connections. Women, who traditionally have not held power, have lots of interests and social connections; men, very few.

Finally, those with the greatest power and freedom desire the least. This is the central tenet of Stoic philosophy and every religion from Buddhism's nonattachment to Jesus' "he who would lose his life will gain it."

If you want nothing that you cannot acquire yourself, then no one can ever hold you, even if you are trapped physically. That is real power. — thegamesmenplay.com

I agree with what most people say: artificial intelligence will be more normalized. I think that it’ll probably start helping with everyday simple tasks. Robots might become cheaper and more common in homes, self-driving cars could eventually replace many cars that we use today, and I think that even space travel might advance and give the chance for ordinary people to go to space. Now obviously, I think everyone would like life to be as comfortable as possible in the future, and if technology is the answer, then I don’t mind it. But I also do think that we shouldn’t rely wholly on technology. If one day it all shuts off, then we will have absolutely no idea how to do simple tasks that are essential to everyday life. I don’t think technology should get so impactful in our lives until we forget to enjoy the world around us, which I think many of us can agree on. But ultimately, I am optimistic for the future ahead of us. While there are many benefits, such as better medicine, technology, transportation, and communications, there are also going to be things that get much worse: pollution, inflation, and maybe possibly war. I think that we should watch the choices we make today, because they will shape our future. I hope 2050 will be a better life than today.
